s: Isolated mountain west of Bisha · proposed Important Plant Area with endemic aloe and dragon trees
te: The lonely mountain of rare plants
se: A lone mountain west of Bisha shelters 118 kinds of plants, including an aloe found only in Saudi Arabia and a few rare dragon trees
sa: جبل منعزل غرب بيشة يحتضن 118 نوعًا من النباتات، منها صبر لا ينمو إلا في السعودية وأشجار دم الأخوين النادرة
desc: Jandaf Mountain is an isolated mountain in the Asir region about 60 km west of Bisha, rising to a summit of 1,910 m above the surrounding Wadi Tarj. A survey in late March 2018 covering about 30 km² recorded 118 plant species in 97 genera and 42 families, mostly perennials. Notable taxa include the national endemic Aloe pseudorubroviolacea, the regional endemic Monolluma quadrangula and the Endangered Dracaena serrulata, of which only about three individuals were found. Annual precipitation is about 126 mm and mean annual temperature about 25 °C. The authors conclude that the mountain meets Important Plant Area and High Conservation Value Area criteria and recommend strict protection.
sig: A small inland mountain whose plant richness rivals much larger areas of the Bisha region, making it a candidate for strict protection.
refs: Al-Namazi, A.A., Algarni, S.M., Wan, J.S.H., Al Mosallam, M.S. & Alotaibi, F. (2022). Floristic composition of Jandaf Mountain as biodiversity hotspot area in southwestern Saudi Arabia. Saudi Journal of Biological Sciences 29, 3654–3660. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sjbs.2022.03.003
conf: Coordinates read as 19°33′N, 42°20′E from the paper’s text, where the degree and minute symbols are lost (printed ‘19330 N, 42200E’); point is the mountain, not a plot. Arabic name is a careful transliteration

s: Juniper-zone park near Tanomah · nesting site of the endangered Asir (Arabian) magpie
el: 1,950 m; four nests found in June 2016
te: Home of the rare blue-black magpie
se: In a mountain park near Tanomah, one of Arabia’s rarest birds, the Asir magpie, still builds its nests
sa: في منتزه جبلي قرب تنومة ما زال العقعق العسيري، أحد أندر طيور الجزيرة العربية، يبني أعشاشه
desc: Al Mehfar park lies about 5 km north-west of Tanomah at 1,950 m in the Asir highlands, within the juniper forest zone. Babbington (2016) recorded one Asir magpie (Pica pica asirensis) there on 22 January 2014, two birds and a nest on 23 May 2014, four birds including two juveniles in July 2014 and four birds in July 2015. No birds were seen in summer 2016, but four nests, two of them new, were found in June 2016. The taxon lives mainly in upland valleys at 1,850–3,000 m, and its breeding population has been estimated at a minimum of 135 pairs; habitat loss from tourism and development and juniper dieback are the main threats.
sig: One of the few recently confirmed breeding places of a magpie found only in the Asir highlands.
disc: At 1,950 m in the juniper zone
refs: Babbington, J. (2016). Update on the status and occurrence of Arabian Magpie Pica pica asirensis in Saudi Arabia. Sandgrouse 38, 146–151. https://osme.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Update-on-the-status-and-occurrence-of-Arabian-Magpie-Pica-pica-asirensis-in-Saudi-Arabia.pdf
conf: Coordinates are the published locality point. Arabic park name is a careful transliteration. The population estimate (Jennings 2010) is quoted by Babbington, who thinks the true number is probably lower

s: Rocky slope in Qilwah · largest recorded stand of the endangered endemic Aloe shadensis
te: The aloe of a single valley
se: On dry rocky slopes in Qilwah grows an aloe found almost nowhere else on Earth, and only a few dozen plants were counted
sa: على منحدرات صخرية جافة في قلوة ينمو صبر يكاد لا يوجد في أي مكان آخر على الأرض، ولم يُحصَ منه إلا بضع عشرات من النباتات
desc: A rocky dry slope in Qilwah Governorate, Al-Bahah, at about 578 m, where a 2022 survey counted 20 individuals of Aloe shadensis, an endangered species endemic to Saudi Arabia. The survey (January–September 2022, 400 m² plots) found the species at only a few sites in the Qilwah and Al-Mukhwah governorates, with an area of occupancy of 20 km² and an extent of occurrence of 188 km², both in the endangered range. Mean annual rainfall is 21.7 mm at Qilwah. The aloe is most abundant on rocky dry slopes facing wadis and is threatened by its low density, narrow range and nearby expanding settlements.
sig: A key locality for one of the most narrowly distributed plants of the Al-Bahah foothills.
refs: Al-Khulaidi, A.W.A. & Alzahrani, F.A. (2023). Geographic distribution of endangered endemic species Aloe shadensis Lavranos & Collen. (Asphodelaceae) in Saudi Arabia. Pakistan Journal of Botany 55(6), 2345–2350. http://dx.doi.org/10.30848/PJB2023-6(32)
conf: Coordinates are the published plot point. The altitude column in the source table is garbled; 578 m is taken from the text. Endangered status is the authors’ assessment from range size

n: Hawala and Jabal Uthrub plant hotspot (Baljurashi)
na: بؤرة التنوع النباتي في حوالة وجبل أثرب (بلجرشي)
s: Sarawat slopes south-west of Baljurashi · 319 plant species, juniper the most frequent
se: On the misty mountain slopes near Baljurashi, scientists counted 319 kinds of plants, with juniper trees the most common
sa: على منحدرات الجبال الضبابية قرب بلجرشي أحصى العلماء 319 نوعًا من النباتات، وكان العرعر أكثرها انتشارًا
desc: A biodiversity hotspot on the Sarawat Mountains near Baljurashi, south-west Al-Bahah, including Hawala, Jabal Uthrub, Al Abna and Huzna, surveyed between April 2017 and July 2018. Ninety-seven 20 × 20 m plots across 167.6 km² recorded 319 plant species in 228 genera and 75 families, including 2 species endemic to Saudi Arabia, 14 near-endemics and 39 rare or endangered species. Juniperus procera was the most frequent species (49% of plots), and Erica arborea occurred above 2,000 m. The richest plots lay on high-altitude slopes around Hawala and the top of Al Abna.
sig: One of the richest documented plant areas of the Arabian Peninsula’s south-western escarpment.
refs: Al-Namazi, A.A., Al-Khulaidi, A.W.A., Algarni, S. & Al-Sagheer, N.A. (2021). Natural plant species inventory of hotspot areas in Arabian Peninsula: Southwest Al-Baha region, Saudi Arabia. Saudi Journal of Biological Sciences 28(6), 3309–3324. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sjbs.2021.02.076
conf: Coordinates are the centre of the published study bounds (about 19.41–19.50° N, 41.29–41.44° E). The paper gives inconsistent elevation ranges and endemic counts; figures here follow its results tables. Arabic spellings of Hawala and Uthrub are careful transliterations

na: الصوان الحامل للذهب في حفة عابث
s: Folded iron-rich chert in Precambrian Arabian Shield rocks north of Al-Bahah · host of ancient gold workings
el: Workings extend more than 120 m down the hillside
se: North of Al-Bahah, ancient miners followed gold through a band of rusty, folded chert squeezed between very old rocks
sa: شمال الباحة تتبّع المعدّنون القدماء الذهب في شريط من الصوان الصدئ المطويّ بين صخور قديمة جدًا
desc: Haffa Abith lies in the southern Wadi Bidah district of the Arabian Shield, in the Jabal Ibrahim and Al Aqiq quadrangles. Gold here occurs in folded ferruginous chert within a Precambrian sequence of carbonaceous schist, carbonate-bearing tuff, dolomitic marble, metabasalt and graywacke, tied to quartz veins, stringers and stockworks. The chert-hosted deposits of the district have low silver and base-metal contents and anomalous arsenic. Ancient open cuts and declines extend more than 120 m down a steep hillside; the site was found by the survey in May 1979.
sig: A clear example of how gold in the Arabian Shield concentrated in iron-rich chert layers of old volcanic-sedimentary basins.
refs: Worl, R.G. & Smith, C.W. (1982). Reconnaissance investigations of ancient gold mines in the southern part of the Wadi Bidah District, Jabal Ibrahim and Al Aqiq quadrangles, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. U.S. Geological Survey Open-File Report 82-789. https://doi.org/10.3133/ofr82789
conf: The source gives only ‘Precambrian’; the timeline uses a broad Neoproterozoic estimate (850–600 Ma). Arabic name is a careful transliteration. Coordinates are from the report text

na: منجم الذهب القديم في بني سار
s: Ancient gold workings along 2.5 km of quartz veins just north of Al-Bahah city
te: The miners’ trench of Bani Sar
se: Near Bani Sar, old miners dug pits, shafts and trenches along gold-bearing quartz veins for more than two and a half kilometres
sa: قرب بني سار حفر المعدّنون القدماء حفرًا وآبارًا وخنادق على امتداد عروق الكوارتز الحاملة للذهب لأكثر من كيلومترين ونصف
desc: The Bani Sar ancient mine lies just north of Al-Bahah city and is one of the few ancient gold mines in the southern Wadi Bidah district that can be reached directly by vehicle. Ancient open cuts, pits and shafts follow a quartz-vein system for more than 2,500 m within a narrow, schistose diorite intrusion about 15 km long. A US Geological Survey team investigated the workings in April 1980 and found the deposit encouraging but in need of more surface work to define its extent. The workings themselves are not dated; archaeological study of Al-Bahah’s mining landscape places Islamic-era mining in the region between the 7th and 12th centuries AD.
sig: Among the most extensive ancient mine workings in the Al-Bahah highlands, linking the region’s rocks to its mining past.
refs: Worl, R.G. & Smith, C.W. (1982). Reconnaissance investigations of ancient gold mines in the southern part of the Wadi Bidah District, Jabal Ibrahim and Al Aqiq quadrangles, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. U.S. Geological Survey Open-File Report 82-789. https://doi.org/10.3133/ofr82789
Al-Zahrani, A.A.A. (2014). Mining in Al-Baha Region, South-Western Saudi Arabia in Islamic-Era: The Archaeology of Asham. PhD thesis, University of York. https://etheses.whiterose.ac.uk/6483/
conf: The Bani Sar workings are undated in the source; the timeline (about AD 600–1150) is a broad estimate from the regional Islamic-era mining dates in Al-Zahrani (2014), not a date for this site. Coordinates are from the USGS report text

s: Permanent river of treated water south of Riyadh · reedbeds and lagoons with over 220 bird species
se: South of Riyadh, treated water keeps a river flowing all year through Wadi Hanifah, drawing herons, eagles and more than 220 kinds of birds
sa: جنوب الرياض تُبقي المياه المعالجة نهرًا جاريًا طوال العام في وادي حنيفة، فيجذب البلشونات والعقبان وأكثر من 220 نوعًا من الطيور
desc: Al-Ha’ir is an artificial, permanently flowing river of treated effluent run-off that runs for about 50 km along Wadi Hanifah, 25 km south of Riyadh, covering a Key Biodiversity Area of 49.8 km² at 480–600 m. The river flows mostly between rocky cliffs, with many pools fringed with reeds and Tamarix, and in places forms wide lagoons between sand dunes beside small pivot-irrigated farms. More than 220 bird species have been recorded, including 20 greater spotted eagles (Aquila clanga) and 17 western marsh harriers (Circus aeruginosus). Little bittern, squacco heron, purple heron and Eurasian reed warbler breed, and black storks winter.
sig: A rare permanent wetland in the arid Najd plateau, important for wintering raptors and breeding herons.
refs: Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership. Al-Ha’ir (KBA 8266) factsheet. https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8266
conf: Coordinates are the KBA central point. Timeline starts from the last assessment (1994); bird counts date from that assessment

s: Desert wadi beside Arar · 196 plant species, mostly annuals after winter rain
te: The wadi that blooms after rain
se: Next to the city of Arar, a dry desert valley bursts into life after winter rain with almost 200 kinds of plants
sa: بجوار مدينة عرعر يدبّ النشاط في وادٍ صحراوي جاف بعد أمطار الشتاء، فتظهر فيه قرابة 200 نوع من النباتات
desc: Wadi Arar is a typical desert wadi of the Northern Borders region next to Arar city, with a hot arid climate, a mean annual temperature of 21.5 °C and about 20.2 mm of rain a year, mostly in winter. Surveys of 25 localities, including its tributaries, between November 2011 and April 2013 recorded 196 plant species in 130 genera and 31 families. Compositae (48 species), Gramineae (26) and Leguminosae (22) were the richest families. Annuals made up 136 species (69.5%) and therophytes 140 species (71.5%), a typical desert spectrum.
sig: A baseline record of the rain-driven desert flora of Saudi Arabia’s far north.
refs: Osman, A.K., Al-Ghamdi, F. & Bawadekji, A. (2014). Floristic diversity and vegetation analysis of Wadi Arar: A typical desert Wadi of the Northern Border region of Saudi Arabia. Saudi Journal of Biological Sciences 21(6), 554–565. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sjbs.2014.02.001
conf: Coordinates are the single study-area point given in the paper. A parallel version (Taeckholmia 34, 2014) gives 194 species; figures here follow the Saudi Journal of Biological Sciences paper. The King Salman Royal Reserve Arar sampling site on the map lies about 7 km away

s: Historic protected rangeland around Faid · 22 reptile species recorded
te: The old protected land of lizards
se: Around the old pilgrim town of Faid, a traditional protected land is home to 17 kinds of lizards and 5 kinds of snakes
sa: حول بلدة فيد القديمة على درب الحجاج يحتضن حمى تقليدي 17 نوعًا من السحالي و5 أنواع من الثعابين
desc: Faid Hema is a historical protected area (hema) of about 4,800 km² around the town of Faid in Ha’il region, about 4.1% of the region’s area; Faid lay on the pilgrimage road between Kufa and Makkah. A survey of five sites from November 2012 to December 2013 recorded 22 reptile species, 17 lizards and 5 snakes, from 134 individuals. Nine species were new records for the hema, and Mesalina adramitana and Walterinnesia aegyptia were first records for Ha’il region. The richest site, Jannin, held about half of all species, while an agricultural site held the fewest; the authors suggest that grazing and hunting control helped keep reptile diversity high.
sig: Shows how a traditional Arabian hema can still conserve desert wildlife.
refs: Alshammari, A.M. & Ibrahim, A.A. (2015). Lizards and Snakes in the Historical Faid Protected Area (Faid Hema), Ha’il Region, Saudi Arabia. Herpetological Conservation and Biology 10(3), 1021–1029. https://lacertilia.de/AF/Bibliografie/BIB_9745.pdf
conf: Coordinates are the centre of the published area bounds (26°20′–27°34′ N, 41°23′–42°31′ E; the paper prints latitude and longitude swapped), so the point is indicative for a large area
